_comment: Watchlist for tooling-rot-siren.sh. Copy to rot-watch.json and edit.
Each entry may set any subset of the keys; omitted keys skip that check.
plugin         plugin id as it appears in installed_plugins.json / enabledPlugins
marketplace    directory name under ~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces (git freshness)
cli            command name on PATH; its --version is compared to the plugin version
stale_days     marketplace freshness threshold, default 14
npm            npm package name; cached registry 'latest' vs the installed version
npm_ttl_hours  how old the cached registry answer may get, default 24
npm_exempt     true = this cli is deliberately not npm-checked (see below)
pin_npm        npm package this PLUGIN hardcodes in its own manifest;
the pin is compared to the registry 'latest'. Needs a
'plugin' key to locate the manifest, and REPORTS when it
matches nothing rather than passing quietly.
pin_files      extra file globs to scan for that same pin, beyond the
plugin manifest: CI workflows, Dockerfiles, scripts. '~'
expands to $HOME. A glob matching ZERO files is a finding.
pin_ref        git ref a stale pin_files hit is cross-checked against, to
tell a stale CHECKOUT from a stale REPO. Default: origin/HEAD,
then origin/main, then main. Consulted only on a hit.
An EMPTY watch array is treated as a finding, not a pass — that is deliberate.
Same reasoning one level up: an entry with a 'cli' but NO 'npm' key skips
the drift check silently, so a half-covered watchlist reports identically
to a fully covered one. The siren therefore flags that entry as PARTIAL
COVERAGE. If the CLI genuinely is not published to npm, say so with
"npm_exempt": true — silence is earned by declaring the gap, never granted
by omitting the key.
Every other check inspects what the machine INSTALLED. A plugin can hardcode
'some-pkg@1.2.3' inside an mcpServers command line and keep spawning 1.2.3
forever while the local CLI floats to latest, with all four other checks green.
That is what pin_npm watches. The pin sits in an args array rather than a named
pin_files is the same idea one layer out: a version written by hand in a repo
file. The manifest scan finds its target through the plugin's installPath, so a
CI workflow is structurally invisible to it — which is how a gate ran a whole
minor version behind everything else on the machine without a word.
field, so the check scans the manifest text for '<package>@<version>'.
The npm check never touches the network on the SessionStart path. It reads
~/.claude/hooks/.rot-npm-cache.json and, when that is missing or older than
npm_ttl_hours, dispatches a DETACHED refresh for the next session. So the
first session after adding an 'npm' key reports cannot-verify, and the one
after that reports real drift. Offline degrades to stale-but-labelled,
never to silence.

watch._comment: Check 5c: a RATCHET BASELINE's instrument stamp, against the version pin_npm actually resolves to. Structurally different from pin_files above, which looks for 'pkg@version' in text -- a stamp is a JSON field holding a bare version string, so no text scan can see it. The case (canary #1048, ten occurrences): CI pins the analyzer to a floating MAJOR, the pin resolves forward on its own, the baseline stamp does not follow, and the ratchet correctly ABSTAINS rather than compare a count against a ceiling measured with a different instrument -- reddening every open PR at once until a human restamps by hand. Exactly one of those ten was cheap: the time this siren noticed first. Needs all three keys: pin_npm names the package to resolve, stamp_key the JSON field, stamp_files the baselines. List EVERY stamped baseline -- they move together, and a finding naming one sends someone to do half the restamp.
